recommendations.regimenLabel: High-dose IV thiamine before glucose + correct magnesium
steps: Give IV THIAMINE BEFORE any glucose (glucose first can precipitate/worsen Wernicke).
High-dose IV thiamine (e.g. 500 mg tds for 2–3 days, then taper) — Pabrinex regimens.
Correct magnesium (cofactor) and other deficiencies; rehydrate.
Treat the underlying cause; alcohol withdrawal management.
Continue oral thiamine after the acute course.

drugRefs.dose: 500 mg three times daily for 2–3 days, then 250 mg daily and taper
drugRefs.duration: 2–3 days IV, then step down to oral
drugRefs.why: Treats established Wernicke's encephalopathy; must be given before any glucose load, which can otherwise precipitate or worsen it. Delivered as Pabrinex (thiamine with other B vitamins).

drugRefs.dose: correct deficiency (e.g. ~2 g IV), guided by serum Mg
drugRefs.why: Magnesium is a cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes; hypomagnesaemia impairs the response to thiamine.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Nutritional Deficiencies / Wernicke's Encephalopathy
EFNS Guidelines for Diagnosis, Therapy and Prevention of Wernicke Encephalopathy
Royal College of Physicians / BNF Guidance on Parenteral B Vitamins (Pabrinex)

recommendations.regimenLabel: Oral maintenance after the acute course

drugRefs.dose: 100 mg once to three times daily
drugRefs.why: Continues repletion after the parenteral course, particularly in ongoing alcohol misuse or malnutrition.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Nutritional Deficiencies / Wernicke's Encephalopathy
EFNS Guidelines for Diagnosis, Therapy and Prevention of Wernicke Encephalopathy

confirm: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia — esp. alcohol misuse or malnutrition. Clinical diagnosis; treat empirically, don't wait for tests.

investigations.test: MRI if uncertain (do not delay treatment)
